alg-csm-frontier-heat-bath-update.definition_interface:
Input a finite nonempty site set $V$, a finite nonempty spin set $S$ with a fixed total order $s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_r$, a strictly positive finite weight $w:S^V\to(0,\infty)$, an initial configuration $x_0\in S^V$, an integer $t\geq0$, a site schedule $i_1,\ldots,i_t\in V$, numbers $u_1,\ldots,u_t\in[0,1]$, and a finite family of observables $f_1,\ldots,f_m:S^V\to\mathbb R$ (the family may be empty). Put $Z=\sum_{x\in S^V}w(x)$ and $\pi(x)=w(x)/Z$. For $i\in V$, an exterior configuration $\eta\in S^{V\setminus\{i\}}$, and $s\in S$, let $\eta^{i,s}\in S^V$ agree with $\eta$ away from $i$ and have spin $s$ at $i$, and set
$$q_i(s\mid\eta)=\frac{w(\eta^{i,s})}{\sum_{a\in S}w(\eta^{i,a})}.$$
The denominator is finite and strictly positive. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, set $\eta=x_{k-1}|_{V\setminus\{i_k\}}$, put $c_0=0$ and $c_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^j q_{i_k}(s_\ell\mid\eta)$, and replace the spin at $i_k$ by the first $s_j$ for which $u_k<c_j$; when $u_k=1$, replace it by $s_r$. Leave every other spin unchanged to obtain $x_k$. Thus the intervals are $[c_{j-1},c_j)$ for $j<r$ and $[c_{r-1},1]$ for $j=r$. Return the trajectory $(x_0,\ldots,x_t)$ and the values $f_a(x_k)$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$ and $k=0,\ldots,t$. For the random-scan heat-bath chain, take the $i_k$ independently uniform on $V$ and the $u_k$ independently uniform on $[0,1]$, with all site and uniform draws mutually independent. The procedure makes no independence claim about successive configurations or observable values.

derivations.claim: For any fixed site $i$, a configuration sampled from $\pi$ has conditional distribution $q_i(\cdot\mid\eta)$ at $i$ given its exterior $\eta$. Replacing its spin by a fresh draw from that same conditional leaves the joint law unchanged: for each $\eta$ and $s$, the resulting mass is $\pi_{V\setminus\{i\}}(\eta)q_i(s\mid\eta)=\pi(\eta^{i,s})$. Averaging these invariant updates over the uniform site choice proves that $\pi$ is invariant for $P$.

For probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set, put $r_s=\min\{p_s,q_s\}$ and $\alpha=\sum_s r_s$. Assign joint mass $r_s$ to $(s,s)$. If $\alpha<1$, add mass $(p_s-r_s)(q_a-r_a)/(1-\alpha)$ to each pair $(s,a)$. The residual supports are disjoint, so this added mass is off the diagonal; summing rows and columns gives marginals $p$ and $q$, and the disagreement probability is $1-\alpha=\frac12\sum_s|p_s-q_s|$. If $\alpha=1$, the diagonal masses alone give the required joint law.

If configurations $x,y$ differ on the set $D=\{j:x_j\ne y_j\}$, then for each site $i$ the triangle inequality, applied while changing the differing exterior coordinates one at a time, gives $\|q_i(\cdot\mid x_{-i})-q_i(\cdot\mid y_{-i})\|_{\rm TV}\leq\sum_{j\in D}c_{ij}$. Use the joint law from step 1.2 to resample the updated spins maximally, and choose the same uniformly random update site in both chains. If $d_H$ is the number of differing coordinates, the expected new Hamming distance is therefore at most $$d_H(x,y)-\frac{d_H(x,y)}n+\frac1n\sum_{j\in D}\sum_i c_{ij}\leq\left(1-\frac{1-c}{n}\right)d_H(x,y).$$ The last inequality uses the column-sum bound in [A1]; the row-sum bound is retained as a stated hypothesis but is not needed for this estimate.

Repeat this joint construction at each update. Conditional expectation and induction give $\mathbb E[d_H(X_t,Y_t)]\leq n(1-(1-c)/n)^t$ when one chain starts at $x$ and the other starts with law $\pi$: initially $d_H\leq n$, and the second marginal remains $\pi$ by step 1.1.

Since $\mathbf1_{\{X_t\ne Y_t\}}\leq d_H(X_t,Y_t)$, for every event $A\subseteq S^V$ the difference $|\Pr(X_t\in A)-\Pr(Y_t\in A)|$ is at most $\Pr(X_t\ne Y_t)$. For finite laws of equal mass, the supremum of this event difference equals half the $\ell^1$ distance: the positive and negative parts of their signed difference have equal mass, each half the sum of absolute values. Taking the supremum over $A$ therefore proves the first total-variation bound in the Statement. For $t=0$ the exponential bound is equality; for $t\geq1$, $(1-u)^t\leq e^{-ut}$ with $u=(1-c)/n\in(0,1]$ gives the stated exponential estimate.

If $a=b$, the observable bound is immediate. Otherwise set $g=(f-a)/(b-a)$, so $0\leq g\leq1$. For the signed measure $\Delta=\mathcal L_x(X_t)-\pi$, the positive and negative masses both equal $\|\Delta\|_{\rm TV}$ because $\Delta(S^V)=0$; hence $|\sum_z g(z)\Delta(z)|\leq\|\Delta\|_{\rm TV}$. Multiplying by $b-a$ and using step 4.1 proves the asserted bias bound.

alg-csm-frontier-monotone-cftp.definition_interface:
Input a finite nonempty set $V$, a set $E\subseteq[V]^2$ of unordered pairs of distinct sites, finite dimensionless couplings $K_e\geq0$, finite dimensionless fields $h_i\in\mathbb R$, and a two-sided iid stream $(I_s,U_s)_{s\in\mathbb Z}$ in which $I_s$ is uniform on $V$, $U_s$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, and all these variables are mutually independent. On $\Omega=\{-1,+1\}^V$, define $\sigma\leq\tau$ by $\sigma_i\leq\tau_i$ for every $i\in V$, using $-1<+1$; its least and greatest elements are $\mathbf{-}$ and $\mathbf{+}$. For the finite-spin heat-bath update, use the total sampling order $+1\prec-1$, which is distinct from $\leq$. Define the strictly positive finite weight
$$w(\sigma)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sum_{i\in V}h_i\sigma_i\right).$$
At time $s$, let $F_s:\Omega\to\Omega$ be the one-site finite-spin heat-bath update at site $I_s$ with uniform value $U_s$, leaving every other spin unchanged; explicitly, site $i$ is set to $+1$ exactly when
$$U_s<\frac{\exp(H_i(\eta))}{\exp(H_i(\eta))+\exp(-H_i(\eta))},\qquad H_i(\eta)=h_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\eta_j,$$
where $\eta$ is the exterior configuration at $i$, and otherwise is set to $-1$. For $T=1,2,4,\ldots$, initialize lower and upper configurations at time $-T$ to $\mathbf{-}$ and $\mathbf{+}$, respectively, and apply in chronological order the same stored maps $F_{-T+1},\ldots,F_0$ to both. If their time-zero outputs agree, return that common configuration. Otherwise double $T$ and replay all maps in the enlarged interval, reusing the already stored maps at every overlapping time. This is a random procedure; no finite running-time bound is part of its definition.

derivations.claim: Every one-site conditional probability of either sign is strictly positive, because it is a ratio of positive finite weights and a positive finite sum. There are only finitely many sites and exterior configurations, so $$\delta=\min_{i\in V,\,\eta\in\{-1,+1\}^{V\setminus\{i\}},\,s\in\{-1,+1\}}q_i(s\mid\eta)>0.$$

For a fixed site $i$, the log odds of the plus conditional are $$\log\frac{q_i(+1\mid\eta)}{q_i(-1\mid\eta)}=2h_i+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}K_{\{i,j\}}\eta_j.$$ If $\eta\leq\zeta$ coordinatewise, the right side for $\eta$ is at most the right side for $\zeta$ because each $K_{\{i,j\}}\geq0$; hence $q_i(+1\mid\eta)\leq q_i(+1\mid\zeta)$. Using the same $U_s$ in both updates therefore preserves coordinatewise order.

The finite Gibbs law $\pi$ is invariant under each heat-bath update: conditional on the spins off site $i$, the original spin and its replacement have the same conditional law $q_i(\cdot\mid\eta)$. Thus replacing the spin preserves every joint probability, and the uniform mixture over sites preserves $\pi$.

Fix an ordering of the $n=|V|$ sites. A block of $n$ successive seeds selects these sites in that order and has every uniform value below $\delta$ with probability $\theta=n^{-n}\delta^n>0$. On that event each update sets its selected spin to $+1$, whatever the other spins are, so the block maps every starting configuration to $\mathbf{+}$. Disjoint blocks in the past are independent; the probability that none of the first $m$ blocks has this event is $(1-\theta)^m\to0$. Thus with probability one a forcing block lies inside some explored horizon. The two extremes then have the same time-zero image, so the doubling procedure terminates almost surely.

Every state lies between $\mathbf{-}$ and $\mathbf{+}$. By step 1.2, applying a shared sequence of update maps preserves these inequalities. If the lower and upper outputs agree, every state started at the same horizon has that common output. The algorithm's returned state is therefore the image of every possible initial state under that finite composition.

For each integer time $t$, almost-sure forcing blocks define $X_t$ as the common image at time $t$ of all initial states started sufficiently far in the past. Intersecting these probability-one events over the countably many integer times defines all $X_t$ simultaneously. The construction is consistent because once a composition maps all states to one value, every earlier extension followed by that composition has the same value. The variable $X_{t-1}$ depends only on seeds through time $t-1$, so it is independent of the seed at time $t$, and $X_t=F_t(X_{t-1})$. The two-sided iid stream is shift-invariant and this construction uses the same rule at every time, so the law $\rho$ of $X_t$ does not depend on $t$. It follows from the definition [L1] that $\rho$ is invariant for $P$.

Put $N=|\Omega|=2^n$. From any state $x$ to any state $y$, the chain can select the fixed site ordering from step 2.1 and set each spin to its value in $y$; this has probability at least $n^{-n}\delta^n>0$. Hence every entry of the $n$-step transition matrix $P^n$ is positive. Let $\kappa=\min_{x,y}P^n(x,y)>0$ and $\lambda=N\kappa\in(0,1]$. If $\lambda<1$, each row of $P^n$ is $\lambda$ times the uniform law on $\Omega$ plus $(1-\lambda)$ times a probability law $R_x$. For any laws $\mu,
u$, the positive and negative parts of $\mu-
u$ each have mass $\|\mu-
u\|_{m TV}$; because $0\leq R_x(A)\leq1$, $|(\mu R)(A)-(
u R)(A)|\leq\|\mu-
u\|_{m TV}$ for every event $A$. Thus $P^n$ contracts total variation by at most $1-\lambda$. If $\lambda=1$, all rows are uniform. In either case two invariant laws for $P$ must coincide. Since $\pi$ is invariant by step 1.3 and $ho$ is invariant by step 3.1, $ho=\pi$.

At time zero, the algorithm returns the common image whenever its explored interval contains a forcing block. By the definition of $X_0$ in step 3.1, this is exactly $X_0$ on the probability-one termination event. Its law is $\rho=\pi$ by step 4.1, proving exactness.

alg-csm-frontier-swendsen-wang.definition_interface: Input a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, an integer $Q\geq2$, finite activities $v_e\geq0$ for $e\in E$, and a spin configuration $\sigma:V\to[Q]$, using the Potts and FK conventions of the finite Potts/FK weight definition. For each edge $e=\{u,v\}$, if $\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)$ set $e$ absent. If $\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)$, draw an independent uniform $U_e\in[0,1]$ and place $e$ in $A$ exactly when $U_e<v_e/(1+v_e)$. For each connected component of $(V,A)$, draw an independent uniform $U_C\in[0,1]$ and assign its vertices the common color $1+\lfloor Q U_C\rfloor$, with the value $Q$ used when $U_C=1$. Return the resulting spin configuration $\sigma'$. The finite graph has finitely many edges and components, so the procedure uses finitely many draws and operations. At $v_e=0$ the edge is never activated; finite $v_e$ ensures the activation probability is less than one.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, and let each edge activity $v_e$ be finite and nonnegative. Use the Potts weight $w_P(\sigma)=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}}(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}})$ and FK weight $w_{FK}(A)=Q^{k_G(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e$ from the finite definitions. Define
$$W(\sigma,A):=\prod_{e\notin A}1\prod_{e\in A}v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}},\qquad (\sigma,A)\in[Q]^V\times2^E.$$
The normalized joint law $\nu(\sigma,A):=W(\sigma,A)/\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$ has Potts marginal $w_P/Z_P$ and FK marginal $w_{FK}/Z_{FK}$, with $Z_P=Z_{FK}=\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$. Conditional on an edge set $A$ of positive probability, the colors of its connected components are independent and uniform on $[Q]$. Thus for every $x,y\in V$,
$$\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=\frac1Q+\left(1-\frac1Q\right)\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y),$$
where $x\leftrightarrow y$ means that $x$ and $y$ lie in the same component of $G_A$.

Input a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, an integer $Q\geq2$, finite activities $v_e\geq0$ for $e\in E$, and a spin configuration $\sigma:V\to[Q]$, using the Potts and FK conventions of the finite Potts/FK weight definition. For each edge $e=\{u,v\}$, if $\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)$ set $e$ absent. If $\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)$, draw an independent uniform $U_e\in[0,1]$ and place $e$ in $A$ exactly when $U_e<v_e/(1+v_e)$. For each connected component of $(V,A)$, draw an independent uniform $U_C\in[0,1]$ and assign its vertices the common color $1+\lfloor Q U_C\rfloor$, with the value $Q$ used when $U_C=1$. Return the resulting spin configuration $\sigma'$. The finite graph has finitely many edges and components, so the procedure uses finitely many draws and operations. At $v_e=0$ the edge is never activated; finite $v_e$ ensures the activation probability is less than one.

derivations.claim: For each fixed spin configuration $\sigma$, summing $W(\sigma,A)$ over $A\subseteq E$ factors over edges. An unequal-spin edge must be absent and contributes $1$; an equal-spin edge contributes either $1$ or $v_e$. Thus $\sum_AW(\sigma,A)=\prod_{e\in E}(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}})=w_P(\sigma)$, which is positive by [F1]. Dividing by this conditional normalizer shows that under $\nu$, given $\sigma$, unequal-spin edges are forced absent and equal-spin edges are independent Bernoulli variables with activation probabilities $v_e/(1+v_e)$, including probability zero when $v_e=0$. This is exactly the first stage of [F3].

Every edge set produced in step 1.1 has $W(\sigma,A)>0$: all active edges have $v_e>0$ and equal endpoint spins, while inactive edges contribute $1$. Therefore $\nu(A)>0$. By [F2], conditional on this edge set, its components receive independent uniform colors. This is exactly the second stage of [F3].

Start with $\sigma$ distributed as the spin marginal $\pi_P$ of $
u$. By step 1.1, after the first stage the pair $(\sigma,A)$ has joint law $
u$. By step 2.1, the new configuration $\sigma'$ is then drawn from the spin conditional law $
u(\cdot\mid A)$. Summing over the finite edge-set space shows that its marginal is the spin marginal of $
u$, namely $\pi_P$. Hence the update preserves $\pi_P$.

The graph has finitely many edges, so the first stage performs one draw per edge; the second stage performs one draw per connected component of a finite graph. Both stages therefore terminate after finitely many operations.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC. The **Metropolis–Hastings procedure** takes as input a standard-Borel
space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), a target
probability measure $\pi$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), and a probability
kernel $Q$ from $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ to itself
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]).

1. On the product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]),
form the proposal-flow measure $\mu$ ([[def-measure]]) on
$\mathsf X\times\mathsf X$ by
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathsf X}Q(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x=\{y:(x,y)\in C\}.$$
This is a probability measure by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].
Let $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$ and set $\mu^{\mathsf T}(C)=\mu(\tau^{-1}C)$.

2. Set $\eta=\mu\wedge\mu^{\mathsf T}$, the greatest measure dominated by both
flows. Put $\lambda_0=\mu+\mu^{\mathsf T}$, which is a finite measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]], and choose nonnegative measurable
representatives $f=d\mu/d\lambda_0$ and $g=d\mu^{\mathsf T}/d\lambda_0$
with $f+g=1$ everywhere after modification on a $\lambda_0$-null set. Define
$$\alpha(x,y)=\begin{cases}\min\{1,g(x,y)/f(x,y)\},&f(x,y)>0,\\1,&f(x,y)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a jointly measurable version of $d\eta/d\mu$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

3. For $x\in\mathsf X$, compute the integrated acceptance probability
$$a(x)=\int_{\mathsf X}\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)$$
and rejection probability $r(x)=1-a(x)$.

4. Return the transition rule
$$P(x,A)=\int_{\mathsf X}\mathbf1_A(y)\alpha(x,y)\,Q(x,dy)+\mathbf1_A(x)r(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal X.$$
The second term retains every rejected proposal as a self-transition.

The item [[lem-common-submeasure-and-bounded-radon-nikodym-density]] proves the
common-submeasure construction and density-version claims in step 2.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[alg-metropolis-hastings-kernel]]. Its output
$P$ is a probability kernel, the joint measure
$J_P(dx,dy)=\pi(dx)P(x,dy)$ is symmetric under $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $\pi$
is invariant for $P$. Symmetry of this joint measure is reversibility. No
irreducibility, uniqueness, convergence-rate, or central limit theorem
conclusion is asserted.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

derivations.claim: The finite discrete metric on $\Omega$ is complete and separable, so [F2] makes it Polish; the identity map then verifies [F1]. The weights sum to $4+\epsilon$, so $\pi$ is a probability measure by [F3]. Each row of $Q$ is nonnegative and sums to one, and on a finite discrete space every function is measurable; thus [F4] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. Consequently the inputs satisfy [F5].

For states $x,y$ with $Q(x,y)>0$, the forward proposal-flow mass is $\mu(x,y)=\pi(x)Q(x,y)$ and the reversed mass is $\mu^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=\pi(y)Q(y,x)$. On a finite set the greatest measure dominated by both has point mass $\min\{\mu(x,y),\mu^{\mathsf T}(x,y)\}$, so [F5] accepts with probability $\min\{1,\pi(y)Q(y,x)/(\pi(x)Q(x,y))\}$. Symmetry of $Q$ reduces this to $\min\{1,e^{-\beta(E(y)-E(x))}\}$. Hence each $L_i$ and $R_i$ jumps to its partner with probability $1/4$, jumps to $H$ with probability $\epsilon/4$, and stays put with probability $3/4-\epsilon/4$; from $H$ it jumps to each of the four well states with probability $1/4$.

By [F6] and [F7], $\pi$ is invariant for $P$. Also $P^4(x,y)>0$ for all $x,y$: every state reaches $L_0$ in at most two positive-probability transitions, $L_0$ reaches every state in at most two, and any unused steps can be filled by the positive self-transition at $L_0$. Since $\Omega$ is finite, let $\kappa=\min_{x,y}P^4(x,y)>0$, $N=|\Omega|=5$, and $\lambda=N\kappa\in(0,1]$. If $\lambda<1$, each row of $P^4$ is $\lambda$ times the uniform law plus $1-\lambda$ times a probability row. For $\Delta=\mu-
u$ with total mass zero, its positive and negative parts each have mass $\|\mu-
u\|_{m TV}$; since every residual row assigns a number in $[0,1]$ to an event, integration against $\Delta$ is bounded in absolute value by $\|\mu-
u\|_{m TV}$. Thus for every two laws $\mu,
u$, $\|\mu P^4-
u P^4\|_{m TV}\leq(1-\lambda)\|\mu-
u\|_{m TV}$. If $\lambda=1$, all rows are uniform. Therefore $\pi$ is the unique invariant law and the chain converges to it.

The target assigns equal mass $1/(4+\epsilon)$ to $L_0,L_1$, so $\pi(\cdot\mid L)$ is uniform and $\pi(L)=2/(4+\epsilon)$. From either state in $L$, the exit probability to $H$ is $\epsilon/4$, while the transition to the other state of $L$ has probability $1/4$. Conditioning a step on no exit gives flip probability $(1/4)/(1-\epsilon/4)=1/(4-\epsilon)$ and stay probability $(3-\epsilon)/(4-\epsilon)$. This symmetric two-state chain preserves the uniform law and has nonconstant eigenvalue $(2-\epsilon)/(4-\epsilon)\leq1/2$, giving the stated within-well total-variation bound. The exit probability is constant across both states, so survival for $t$ steps has probability $(1-\epsilon/4)^t$.

Survival implies $X_t\in L$, so for the initial law $\pi(\cdot\mid L)$, $\Pr(X_t\in L)\geq(1-\epsilon/4)^t$. On a finite space, if $\Delta=\mu-\nu$ has total mass zero then $\sup_A|\Delta(A)|=\frac12\sum_x|\Delta(x)|$, so the event $L$ gives $$\|\pi(\cdot\mid L)P^t-\pi\|_{\rm TV}\geq(1-\epsilon/4)^t-\pi(L).$$ For any mixture of starting states, the half-$\ell^1$ triangle inequality bounds its distance from $\pi$ by the largest component distance. Since $\pi(\cdot\mid L)P^t$ is the mixture of $P^t(L_0,\cdot)$ and $P^t(L_1,\cdot)$ with weights $1/2$, it follows that $d(t)\geq(1-\epsilon/4)^t-2/(4+\epsilon)$. If $t\leq\lfloor\epsilon^{-1}\rfloor$, Bernoulli's inequality gives $(1-\epsilon/4)^t\geq1-t\epsilon/4\geq3/4$, while $2/(4+\epsilon)<1/2$; hence $d(t)\geq1/4>1/8$. The definition of $t_{\rm mix}(1/8)$ therefore gives the claimed lower bound.

ex-csm-frontier-metastable-diagnostic.definition_interface:
Assume AC. Fix $\beta>0$ in reciprocal-energy units and a finite barrier height $B>0$ in the corresponding energy unit, so $\beta B$ is dimensionless; put $\epsilon=e^{-\beta B}\in(0,1)$, and let the five states be $\Omega=\{L_0,L_1,H,R_0,R_1\}$. The energies are $E(L_0)=E(L_1)=E(R_0)=E(R_1)=0$ and $E(H)=B$, so the Gibbs law is $\pi(x)=e^{-\beta E(x)}/(4+\epsilon)$. Let $Q$ be the symmetric proposal matrix specified by
$$Q(L_i,L_i)=Q(R_i,R_i)=\frac12,\quad Q(L_i,L_{1-i})=Q(R_i,R_{1-i})=\frac14,\quad Q(L_i,H)=Q(R_i,H)=\frac14\quad(i=0,1),$$
and $Q(H,x)=1/4$ for $x\in\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$, with all other entries zero. Each row sums to one. Apply the Metropolis–Hastings procedure with target $\pi$ and proposal $Q$, and denote its transition matrix by $P$. Write $L=\{L_0,L_1\}$ for the left well and define
$$d(t)=\max_{x\in\Omega}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\rm TV},\qquad \|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}=\frac12\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|.$$
The Gibbs law is invariant, but the chain started with law $\pi(\cdot\mid L)$ has probability $(1-\epsilon/4)^t$ of making no exit from $L$ during its first $t$ steps. Conditional on no exit, its two-state within-well transition flips between $L_0$ and $L_1$ with probability $1/(4-\epsilon)$; the conditional stationary law within the well is uniform, and from either state its within-well total-variation error after $t$ such updates is at most $\frac12((2-\epsilon)/(4-\epsilon))^t\leq2^{-t-1}$. Nevertheless,
$$d(t)\geq(1-\epsilon/4)^t-\frac{2}{4+\epsilon}\geq\frac14\qquad\text{for every integer }0\leq t\leq\lfloor\epsilon^{-1}\rfloor.$$
Thus the conventional worst-start mixing time $t_{\rm mix}(1/8):=\min\{t:d(t)\leq1/8\}$ exceeds $\lfloor e^{\beta B}\rfloor$, even though the chain can equilibrate quickly within one well. This is an exact finite mathematical example; it reports no simulated or measured data.
